newsitem.title: INDIA: COMMODITIES - Dull response to India coffee auctions.
newsitem.headline: COMMODITIES - Dull response to India coffee auctions.

text.p: India resumed coffee auctions last week after a three-month break but the response from exporters was poor due to a holiday season in Europe, traders said on Sunday.
The Indian Coffee Trade Association (ICTA) suspended auctions on April 1 after the southern state of Karnataka imposed a three percent turnover tax on coffee dealers and brokers.
"The tax issue has been resolved. But the auction last Wednesday drew little response," said Arun Bidappa, chief executive of the Karnataka Coffee Brokers Pvt Ltd.
He said the months of June and July were generally dull for the coffee business in Europe and the United States because of the holiday season.
"The market is expected to revive by mid-August. I expect coffee prices to firm to 200 cents per pound from the present 175/180 cents," Bidappa said.

ICTA started conducting auctions in October 1995 after the state-run Coffee Board stopped direct marketing operations. Bidappa's Karnataka Brokers is one of four firms involved in holding the auctions.
Bidappa said the four-month June-September monsoon had so far been normal and beneficial to the coffee crop.

"But the rainfall has been slightly lower than in the previous year," Bidappa said. The 1997/98 (Oct/Sept) crop is expected to be around 220,000 tonnes, up from the previous year's 180,000 tonnes, he said.
In other commodities, unabated imports of palmolein, sparked by a dip in international prices, have offset a drop in local supplies and brought down domestic prices, traders said.
"About 10,000 tonnes of imported oil is arriving at Bombay port every week," said Navin Shah, president of the Bombay Oilseeds and Oils Exchange.
Industry officials said about 125,000 tonnes of edible oil imports arrived in June. Imports in July are expected to be around 150,000 tonnes, they said.
In the week to Friday, palmolein prices dropped three rupees to 263 rupees per 10 kg. Groundnut oil, however, firmed two rupees to 355 rupees per 10 kg.
Gold's plunge to a 12-year low last week had little impact on demand in India, the world's largest importer of the yellow metal, dealers said.
On the London market, gold fell below $325 an ounce on Friday after news that Australia's central bank had sold bullion from its reserves.
"We are passing through a lean period. The movement of world prices has had no impact on demand for gold," said M.L. Damani, president of the Bombay Bullion Association.
Gold standard (24 carats) crashed 220 rupees to 4,365 rupees per 10 grammes in the week to Friday.
Dealers said demand for gold in the three months of June, July and August is always dull because buyers in rural areas are busy sowing crops with the onset of the monsoon.
The progress of the monsoon has been satisfactory in central India, where sowing was over in 40 percent of the area under soybean cultivation, estimated at 5.7 million hectares, traders said.
They said higher soybean prices in 1996/97 (Nov/Oct) had induced farmers to step up the area under cultivation from 5.0 million hectares for the 1997/98 season.
Traders said overseas demand for soymeal had been dull and pushed domestic prices sharply down during the week.
They said soymeal exports were quoted at $255-257 per tonne FAS (free alongside ship) against $268-270 last week.
"Soymeal export prices have fallen by about $65 per tonne in the past one month due to lack of export demand," said a trader.
Cotton prices too came under pressure with the progress of the monsoon, traders said.
Supplies of cotton will be enough to keep prices down till October, when the new crop arrives, they said.
Traders said state procurement agencies held enough stocks as carryover for the 1997/98 (Oct/Sept) season.
Traders said some cotton sown early in the southern state of Karnataka and the western state of Gujarat was expected to arrive on the market by the end of July.
Traders said they expected prices to remain easy. The bulk of the current season's crop, estimated at 16.78 bales (170 kg each) had already been marketed, they said.
